bull_bear.body: Self-funded growth (net cash + OCF); no equity dilution. Discipline: any new vertical must clear >20% ROCE (contract manufacturing included). Working-capital rationalization (advances to mills to secure supply amid geopolitics) as scale builds.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Geopolitics/steel-price volatility:** Iran-US war reignited ~10 days pre-call; oil→steel/commodity volatility; a March-style fuel/gas shortage would hurt customer industries and sales broadly ("nothing specific to us").
- **Coated-steel dependency** on third parties until Raipur commissions (18 months) — execution/slippage risk.
- **Seasonality** in service-center volumes (Q1 QoQ dip).
- **Mix-driven EBITDA/ton variability** (management won't guide per-ton QoQ).
- Rapid multi-vertical expansion execution risk.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident, granular, disclosure-forward (added segmental splits; accepted analyst suggestion to publish per-segment EBITDA). Careful not to over-promise per-ton margins; reframes the "25 vs 30 service centers" target as coverage-of-industrial-clusters rather than a number. Repeatedly anchors credibility to the APL Apollo track record. Candid that a macro shock is the one real caveat to the Rs 300 cr EBITDA guide.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The margin uplift is *real*, not cyclical: absolute inventory fell Rs 284→209 cr into rising steel prices, so there is little inventory-gain flatter in the >4% EBITDA margin.
- Backward integration is the whole thesis — it converts a Rs 3,000-4,000/t bought-coated-steel business into a Rs 6,000-7,000/t integrated one; the 18-month Raipur timeline is the single most important milestone.
- Trading is being deliberately zeroed out of the 2030 volume vision (4 mn t of the target is "0 t trading") — a quality-over-volume signal often missed by those anchoring on the old aggregator model.
- Contract manufacturing (details next quarter) is a new, potentially large optionality not yet in numbers.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Net cash of Rs 6.9 Bn as at 30 June 2026, having built from Rs 4.6 Bn in FY25 to Rs 7.5 Bn in FY26, giving self-funding capacity for the network build-out.
- Debt reduced from Rs 2,314 Mn at FY26-end to Rs 1,075 Mn, against shareholders' funds of Rs 16,431 Mn — a largely equity-funded balance sheet.
- Growth has been part-funded by equity, with a capital increase of Rs 2,773 Mn in FY26 versus Rs 10 Mn in Q1FY27.
- No dividend payments in FY26 or Q1FY27; free cash flow is being reinvested into capex, with FY26 FCF of Rs 142 Mn and Q1FY27 FCF of negative Rs 657 Mn.
- Management frames capital allocation philosophy as 'efficient capital allocation' alongside disciplined execution and operational excellence.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Established industry linkages — long-standing relationships with steel producers and annual MOUs with key steel manufacturers ensure reliable sourcing and supply continuity across cycles
- Integrated business model spanning trading, service centres, distribution and renewables, providing value chain control and customer stickiness
- Scale and financial strength — described as a net cash company with a capital base supporting service centre expansion, capacity addition and working capital needs
- Diversified product portfolio with over 7,200 SKUs, reducing reliance on pure trading
- Growing customer and supplier network — over 2,470 customers and 452 vendors onboarded by end-FY26, with supplier additions including NMDC and JSOL
- In-house manufacturing and tooling capability in solar structures, giving control over production, quality and turnaround times, with repeat orders from EPC firms and IPPs
- SAP-enabled production and inventory management with defined service lead times, improving order execution visibility
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Volatility in steel prices — Fluctuations in steel prices can lead to inventory losses, margin pressure and earnings volatility, particularly given the working capital-intensive nature of operations. The Company states that, as highlighted in recent performance, sharp corrections impacted EBITDA due to inventory holding cycles, and the MD&A notes margins were impacted during the period due to softness in demand and correction in steel prices. Mitigation cited: dynamic pricing, reduction in inventory holding cycles, and a greater contribution from higher-margin service centre and renewable structure segments.
- Working capital intensity of an inventory-led trading model — Listed as a weakness in the SWOT: inventory-led operations and supplier advances may impact return ratios if not tightly managed. The ratio commentary attributes lower debtors' and inventory turnover to higher trade receivables and higher average inventory during the year, compounding the exposure to price swings.
- Increasing competition in a fragmented B2B construction-materials ecosystem — The B2B ecosystem remains highly fragmented with increasing participation from organised platforms and digital aggregators, potentially exerting pressure on market share, pricing power and customer retention. Mitigation cited: continuous monitoring of competitive dynamics and pricing benchmarks, strengthening supplier relationships, widening the customer base and differentiating on standardised pricing, quality assurance and integrated supply solutions.
- Digital disruption of the traditional trading model — A gradual industry shift towards digital procurement platforms and organised marketplaces may reduce reliance on conventional trading models, impacting the long-term growth trajectory. Mitigation cited: shifting product mix towards value-added segments such as processing, distribution and specialty products, and strengthening platform-led capabilities.
- Supply chain and logistics disruption, including supplier concentration — The business model relies on seamless procurement and distribution of steel and construction materials; transportation constraints, supplier concentration or geopolitical factors may impact delivery timelines and operational efficiency. The BRSR materiality table reinforces this: as a trading and distribution business the Company does not control upstream production, so continuity of supply and its environmental and labour footprint depend heavily on third-party manufacturers and mills, and overreliance on a narrow supplier base creates both disruption and reputational risk.
- Operational bottlenecks from rapid expansion — Rapid expansion of service centres, product lines and geographies may lead to inefficiencies in inventory management, coordination challenges and execution risks, impacting service levels and margins. Mitigation cited: advanced inventory management systems, process standardisation, monitoring of operational KPIs and investment in logistics infrastructure and workforce capability.
- Product quality, safety and standards compliance in traded construction materials — Core trade is in structural and construction-grade steel products (TMT bars, HR coils/sheets, structural sections) alongside tiles, sanitaryware and electrical fittings. Because these are safety-critical, load-bearing or life-safety-relevant inputs, a certification or quality lapse at the manufacturer level can translate into construction-site safety risk and legal/reputational exposure for the Company as the distribution channel, even though it does not manufacture the goods. Mitigation cited: sourcing exclusively from BIS-certified and reputed brand manufacturers, quality verification at warehouses and service centres, and product traceability from source to dealer.
- Talent capability and workforce stability against a lean employee base — The BRSR materiality table states the Company operates with a comparatively lean corporate workforce relative to the scale and geographic spread of goods it moves, spanning commercial, supply-chain and finance functions; the MD&A reports a total of 177 employees as of March 31, 2026. As the Company grows and diversifies into new product categories, its ability to attract, train and retain capable talent is a key determinant of execution quality and growth sustainability.
- Technological disruption and cyber risk in a platform-dependent model — Dependence on digital platforms and IT infrastructure exposes operations to system failures, cyber threats and data integrity issues that could disrupt business continuity and stakeholder trust. Mitigation cited: IT governance frameworks, periodic system upgrades, cybersecurity protocols, real-time monitoring, regular audits, data backup and disaster recovery planning.
- Cyclical demand and regulatory/trade-policy change — Demand is linked to construction and infrastructure spending and remains sensitive to economic conditions, while changes in trade policies, duties or sector regulations may impact cost structures and operations. Separately, the Company flags regulatory and compliance risk arising from operating in a regulated environment requiring adherence to SEBI (LODR), taxation and other statutory norms, where non-compliance may result in penalties and reputational impact. The Directors' Report adds a measured FY27 outlook citing geopolitical risks, trade disruptions, soft urban demand and inflationary pressures.

business.body:

business.body:
- Positions itself as an integrated building and infrastructure materials platform (one-stop shop) offering construction solutions from top brands under one roof, rather than a pure trading intermediary.
- Business model rests on five stated pillars: manufacturing, brand partnerships, strategically located service centres, an extensive distribution network, and an online marketplace for sourcing building materials.
- Customer base spans top-tier EPC companies, real estate developers, OEMs, Independent Power Producers, traders, dealers and retailers, with 2,505 registered customers by end-Q1FY27 versus 2,312 a year earlier.
- Target industries are renewables, infrastructure, industrials, and residential and commercial construction, giving diversified exposure across construction demand pools.
- Formerly known as Kintech Renewables Limited; registered in Delhi with corporate office at Noida.

business.body: SG Mart supplies metals and building materials, including steel products such as hot rolled coils, billets, TMT bars and structural steel, to customers across construction, industrial, infrastructure and manufacturing applications. Operations are organised across four business verticals: B2B metal trading, a network of service centres, Steel Profiling Products and solar structures, allowing participation from bulk sourcing and trading through value-added processing to downstream distribution. The Company procures bulk metal directly from primary producers and supplies dealers, distributors and industrial buyers, supported by a pan-regional network of warehouses and service centres.

- **Service Centres:** Metal Plates, Embossed sheets
- **Steel Profiling Products:** Door Frames, Racking Profiles, Cable Trays, Strut Channels, Z/C Purlins
- **Solar Structures:** Utility industrial solar mounting structures, Residential solar mounting structures, Solar Module Mounting Structures
- **Downstream / value-added:** TMT bars, Structural steel, Structural solutions

outlook.body:
- **FY27 EBITDA ~Rs 300 cr (absolute)** — reaffirmed from Q4 call; only caveat is a macro/geopolitical shock. Absolute EBITDA to grow every quarter (blended EBITDA/ton may wobble on mix).
- **Revenue growth ~50% CAGR** over next 3 years (analyst-stated, management-owned as target).
- **Service centers: 25 by 2029** (from 7; +5/yr); **12 operational within 6-12 months** (7 new already under construction, land/cities identified).
- **Raipur backward integration (coated steel): operational in ~18 months** → profile/renewable EBITDA/ton to Rs 6,000-7,000 (from Rs 3,000-4,000); +Rs 3,000-4,000/t uplift.
- **Profiles + renewables: 3.5-4x volume growth** in 2-3 years (120k t run-rate today vs 400k t installed capacity).
- **7 new products** to launch over Q2-Q3 FY27 (capacity already in place); new **contract-manufacturing** category — details next quarter.
- **Working capital: 27 days → 20-25 days** within 2 years (backward integration cuts raw-material stocking).
- **Vision 2030:** 4-4.5 mn tons; revenue Rs 25,000-35,000 cr; EBITDA min Rs 1,000 cr (3-4% margin) — 3 mn t service centers + ~1 mn t profiles/renewables, ~0 t trading.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Build a scalable and margin-accretive business by aligning operations with high-potential segments and maintaining disciplined execution, having transitioned from an exploratory phase to a more structured model
- Focus on Value-Added Segments — expanding beyond pure trading into segments that offer stronger margins and customer engagement
- Rationalisation of Capital-Intensive Models — reducing exposure to models with high cash burn by prioritising businesses with stronger unit economics and tighter control over working capital
- Leveraging Group Expertise — drawing on over three decades of experience within the broader ecosystem to guide execution and decision-making
- Invest over ₹1,500 crore in the next three years in new service centres, land acquisition and additional profiling machines, funded through internal accruals and the net cash position without material dilution
- Reposition B2B metal trading within a broader integrated platform across the metals value chain, combining sourcing, processing and distribution to strengthen control over product flow and increase participation in value-added segments
- Scale the service centre vertical by expanding processing capabilities (slitting lines added) and moving into downstream value-added products such as CRCA and GP
- Shift Steel Profiling Products from a trading-led model to a white-labelling and franchise-based royalty model, expanding the franchise, distributor and channel-partner network
- Build out the solar structures vertical with in-house manufacturing and tooling, expanding into rooftop solar structures and deepening relationships with EPC firms and IPPs
- Evolve towards a more structured operating model with a sharper focus on identified growth drivers, aiming to build a scalable and profitable platform as the Company progresses towards 2030
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: SG Mart operates a pan-regional network of warehouses and service centres, with 7 operational service centres and 7,200+ SKUs as disclosed in the MD&A company overview. The Directors' Report states the Company plans to add three to four additional centres in FY27, with opportunities actively being evaluated in Hyderabad, Chennai and Punjab. Alongside the service centre build-out, the Company is expanding into application-led segments such as solar structures and steel profiles, and is undertaking backward integration initiatives including zinc coating to enhance value realisation. In the Steel Profiling Products vertical the stated intent is to scale capacity to 0.5 MTPA alongside further expansion of the distribution network and deeper engagement with channel partners, having transitioned that vertical from a trading-led model to a white-labelling and franchise-based royalty model with increased franchise onboarding during the year. In solar structures, the Company expanded its presence into rooftop solar structures and established a distribution network, operates in-house manufacturing capabilities across locations supported by advanced machinery and dedicated in-house tooling workshops, and aims to expand capacity up to 0.5 MTPA through ongoing capacity additions, scaling its presence significantly over the next two to three years. The MD&A strengths and opportunities commentary cites ongoing addition of service centres across geographies as an opportunity expected to improve volumes and operating leverage, and notes that a strong capital base supports expansion of service centres, capacity addition and working capital needs. Separately, the BRSR Principle 2 disclosure states the Company made capital investments in rainwater harvesting systems, alcohol breath analysers, fire safety equipment and water purification systems; such sustainability-linked capex was 0.04% of total capex in FY 2025-26 versus 0.2% in FY 2024-25. No rupee quantum for the overall capex programme is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's construction industry — valued at USD 685 billion in FY 2025 and estimated to reach around USD 1,245.7 billion by FY 2034 (CAGR 6.8%) — driven by sustained government capital expenditure, rising urbanisation and investment in roads, railways, metro projects and energy
- Indian real estate momentum, valued at approximately USD 532.6 billion in 2025 and projected to reach around USD 1.26 trillion by 2034 (CAGR 10%), with increasing traction in Tier II and Tier III cities broadening the demand base
- Structural shift in the Indian B2B building materials market driven by a capital expenditure push and rapid industry formalisation, moving procurement from fragmented local sourcing to organised, high-volume supply chain networks; the infrastructure and construction goods segment recorded double-digit growth of 13.7%
- Rapid digitalisation of B2B trade, with e-commerce accounting for nearly 30% of contractor order volumes and buyers moving to unified digital platforms prioritising pricing transparency and multi-warehouse inventory management
- Renewable energy expansion — India crossing over 50% non-fossil-fuel installed power capacity ahead of its 2030 targets, with a record 55.29 GW added during FY 2025-26 — supporting demand for solar mounting structures
- Indian steel industry growth, with crude steel production at 168.4 million tonnes (up 10.7%) and consumption at 163.7 million tonnes (up 7.6%) in FY 2025-26, supported by infrastructure, construction and manufacturing demand
- Government capital expenditure allocation of approximately INR 12.2 lakh crore (about 3.1% of GDP) in the Union Budget FY 2025-26, accelerating investment under PM GatiShakti and the National Infrastructure Pipeline
- Margin lever from progressively rebalancing the business mix towards higher-margin value-added and application-driven segments (service centres, steel profiling, solar structures) and away from low-margin B2B trading
- B2B metal trading demand remained robust with stronger momentum observed in the second half of the year, though segment volumes and revenues stabilised at lower levels reflecting a calibrated trading approach
- Management flags a measured outlook: FY27 growth projected at 6.8%-7.2%, with geopolitical risks, trade disruptions, soft urban demand and inflationary pressures as watch items, alongside input cost volatility and cyclical demand fluctuations
- Solar structures: strengthened relationships with EPC firms and IPPs, reflected in repeat orders and a steadily expanding network within this segment
- Steel Profiling Products: distributor engagement strengthened through branding support and facilitation of project approvals, enhancing order visibility and market responsiveness
- Service centres: order fulfilment processes strengthened through defined service lead times and SAP-based production and inventory management, improving visibility and control over order execution
- No quantified order book or order-inflow value is disclosed in this section
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Second consecutive quarter proving the trading→manufacturing pivot: blended EBITDA margin now >4% (~4.5%), annualized ROCE ~23%, on a net-cash Rs 690 cr balance sheet — with management stressing this is *structural*, not inventory-gain (absolute inventory actually fell to Rs 209 cr from Rs 284 cr despite Rs 2,500-3,000/ton steel-price inflation). The four value-added verticals (service centers, steel profiles, renewable structures, accessories) are being scaled toward a 2030 vision of 4-4.5 mn tons and Rs 25,000-35,000 cr revenue / Rs 1,000 cr+ EBITDA. The margin step-up lever is a Raipur backward-integration (coated-steel) line, operational in ~18 months, taking profile/renewable EBITDA/ton from Rs 3,000-4,000 to Rs 6,000-7,000.

The ratio commentary attributes lower debtors' and inventory turnover to higher trade receivables and higher average inventory during the year, compounding the exposure to price swings.
risks.risk: Working capital intensity of an inventory-led trading model

risks.note: The B2B ecosystem remains highly fragmented with increasing participation from organised platforms and digital aggregators, potentially exerting pressure on market share, pricing power and customer retention. Mitigation cited: continuous monitoring of competitive dynamics and pricing benchmarks, strengthening supplier relationships, widening the customer base and differentiating on standardised pricing, quality assurance and integrated supply solutions.
risks.risk: Increasing competition in a fragmented B2B construction-materials ecosystem

risks.note: A gradual industry shift towards digital procurement platforms and organised marketplaces may reduce reliance on conventional trading models, impacting the long-term growth trajectory. Mitigation cited: shifting product mix towards value-added segments such as processing, distribution and specialty products, and strengthening platform-led capabilities.
risks.risk: Digital disruption of the traditional trading model

risks.note: The business model relies on seamless procurement and distribution of steel and construction materials; transportation constraints, supplier concentration or geopolitical factors may impact delivery timelines and operational efficiency. The BRSR materiality table reinforces this: as a trading and distribution business the Company does not control upstream production, so continuity of supply and its environmental and labour footprint depend heavily on third-party manufacturers and mills, and overreliance on a narrow supplier base creates both disruption and reputational risk.
risks.risk: Supply chain and logistics disruption, including supplier concentration

risks.note: Rapid expansion of service centres, product lines and geographies may lead to inefficiencies in inventory management, coordination challenges and execution risks, impacting service levels and margins. Mitigation cited: advanced inventory management systems, process standardisation, monitoring of operational KPIs and investment in logistics infrastructure and workforce capability.

Core trade is in structural and construction-grade steel products (TMT bars, HR coils/sheets, structural sections) alongside tiles, sanitaryware and electrical fittings. Because these are safety-critical, load-bearing or life-safety-relevant inputs, a certification or quality lapse at the manufacturer level can translate into construction-site safety risk and legal/reputational exposure for the Company as the distribution channel, even though it does not manufacture the goods. Mitigation cited: sourcing exclusively from BIS-certified and reputed brand manufacturers, quality verification at warehouses and service centres, and product traceability from source to dealer.
risks.risk: Product quality, safety and standards compliance in traded construction materials

risks.note: The BRSR materiality table states the Company operates with a comparatively lean corporate workforce relative to the scale and geographic spread of goods it moves, spanning commercial, supply-chain and finance functions; the MD&A reports a total of 177 employees as of March 31, 2026. As the Company grows and diversifies into new product categories, its ability to attract, train and retain capable talent is a key determinant of execution quality and growth sustainability.
risks.risk: Talent capability and workforce stability against a lean employee base
